source_text: Πρὸ δὲ τῆς εἰς τὸ προκείμενον ἐγχειρήσεως ἐν προοιμίου εἴδει προσαποδοτέον τῷ πέρατι τοῦ πέμπτου Στρωματέως τὰ ἐνδέοντα. Ἐπεὶ γὰρ παρεστήσαμεν τὸ συμβολικὸν εἶδος ἀρχαῖον εἶναι, κεχρῆσθαι δὲ αὐτῷ οὐ μόνον τοὺς προφήτας τοὺς παρ’ ἡμῖν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν Ἑλλήνων τῶν παλαιῶν τοὺς πλείονας καὶ τῶν ἄλλων τῶν κατὰ τὰ ἔθνη βαρβάρων οὐκ ὀλίγους, ἐχρῆν δὲ καὶ τὰ μυστήρια ἐπελθεῖν τῶν τελουμένων· ταῦτα μὲν ὑπερτίθεμαι διασαφήσων, ὁπηνίκα ἂν τὰ περὶ ἀρχῶν τοῖς Ἕλλησιν εἰρημένα ἐπιόντες διελέγχωμεν· τῆσδε γὰρ ἔχεσθαι τῆς θεωρίας ἐπιδείξομεν καὶ τὰ μυστήρια· παραστήσαντες δὲ τὴν ἔμφασιν τῆς Ἑλληνικῆς διανοίας ἐκ τῆς διὰ τῶν γραφῶν εἰς ἡμᾶς δεδομένης ἀληθείας περιαυγασθεῖσαν, καθ’ ὃ σημαινόμενον διήκειν εἰς αὐτοὺς τὴν κλοπὴν τῆς ἀληθείας ἐκδεχόμενοι, εἰ μὴ ἐπαχθὲς εἰπεῖν, ἀπεδείξαμεν, φέρε μάρτυρας τῆς κλοπῆς αὐτοὺς καθ’ ἑαυτῶν παραστήσωμεν τοὺς Ἕλληνας· οἱ γὰρ τὰ οἰκεῖα οὕτως ἄντικρυς παρ’ ἀλλήλων ὑφαιρούμενοι βεβαιοῦσι μὲν τὸ κλέπται εἶναι, σφετερίζεσθαι δ’ ὅμως καὶ ἄκοντες τὴν παρ’ ἡμῶν ἀλήθειαν εἰς τοὺς ὁμοφύλους λάθρᾳ διαδείκνυνται. οἱ γὰρ μηδὲ ἑαυτῶν, σχολῇ γε τῶν ἡμετέρων ἀφέξονται. καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ φιλοσοφίαν σιωπήσομαι δόγματα, αὐτῶν ὁμολογούντων ἐγγράφως τῶν τὰς αἱρέσεις διανεμομένων, ὡς μὴ ἀχάριστοι ἐλεγχθεῖεν, παρὰ Σωκράτους εἰληφέναι τὰ κυριώτατα τῶν δογμάτων. ὀλίγοις δὲ τῶν καθωμιλημένων καὶ παρὰ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν εὐδοκίμων ἀνδρῶν χρησάμενος μαρτυρίοις, τὸ κλεπτικὸν διελέγξας εἶδος αὐτῶν, ἀδιαφόρως τοῖς χρόνοις καταχρώμενος, ἐπὶ τὰ ἑξῆς τρέψομαι. Ὀρφέως τοίνυν ποιήσαντος· ὣς οὐ κύντερον ἦν καὶ ῥίγιον ἄλλο γυναικός, Ὅμηρος ἄντικρυς λέγει· ὣς οὐκ αἰνότερον καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο γυναικός. Γράψαντός τε Μουσαίου· ὡς αἰεὶ τέχνη μέγ’ ἀμείνων ἰσχύος ἐστίν, Ὅμηρος λέγει· μήτι τοι δρυτόμος περιγίνεται ἠὲ βίηφι. Πάλιν τοῦ Μουσαίου ποιήσαντος· ὡς δ’ αὔτως καὶ φύλλα φύει ζείδωρος ἄρουρα· ἄλλα μὲν ἐν μελίῃσιν ἀποφθίνει, ἄλλα δὲ φύει· ὣς δὲ καὶ ἀνθρώπων γενεὴν καὶ φῦλον ἑλίσσει, Ὅμηρος μεταγράφει· φύλλα τὰ μέν τ’ ἄνεμος χαμάδις χέει, ἄλλα δέ θ’ ὕλη τηλεθόωσα φύει, ἔαρος δ’ ἐπιγίνεται ὥρη· ὣς ἀνδρῶν γενεὴ ἣ μὲν φύει, ἣ δ’ ἀπολήγει. Πάλιν δ’ αὖ Ὁμήρου εἰπόντος· οὐχ ὁσίη κταμένοισιν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι, Ἀρχίλοχός τε καὶ Κρατῖνος γράφουσιν, ὃ μέν· οὐ γὰρ ἐσθλὰ κατθανοῦσι κερτομεῖν ἐπ’ ἀνδράσιν, Κρατῖνος δὲ ἐν τοῖς Λάκωσι· φοβερὸν ἀνθρώποις τόδ’ αὖ, κταμένοις ἐπ’ αἰζηοῖσιν καυχᾶσθαι μέγα. Αὖθίς τε ὁ Ἀρχίλοχος τὸ Ὁμηρικὸν ἐκεῖνο μεταφέρων· ἀασάμην, οὐδ’ αὐτὸς ἀναίνομαι· ἀντί νυ πολλῶν, ὧδέ πως γράφει· ἤμβλακον, καί πού τινα ἄλλον ἥδ’ ἄτη κιχήσατο· καθάπερ ἀμέλει κἀκεῖνο τὸ ἔπος· ξυνὸς ἐνυάλιος, καί τε κτανέοντα κατέκτα, μεταποιῶν αὐτὸς ὧδέ πως ἐξήνεγκεν· † ἔρξω· ἐτήτυμον γὰρ ξυνὸς ἀνθρώποιςιν Ἄρης. ἔτι κἀκεῖνο μεταφράζων· νίκης ἀνθρώποισιν θεῶν ἐν † πείρᾳ κεῖται, διὰ τοῦδε τοῦ ἰάμβου δῆλός ἐστι· καὶ νέους θάρρυνε, νίκης δὲ ἐν θεοῖσι πείρατα.
pass_a_gloss: But before the attempt at the proposed task, it is necessary to give back to the end of the fifth Stromata what is fitting. For since we have shown that the symbolic type is ancient and that not only our prophets but also most of the ancient Greeks and not a few of the other barbarian nations have used it, it was necessary also to examine the mysteries of the initiations; these things I pass over for now, explaining them when we come to the things said by the Greeks about first principles; for we will show that they have this theory and the mysteries. Having shown the emphasis of the Greek mind, illuminated by the truth given to us through the scriptures, and having indicated that they have received the theft of truth from us, if it is not unpleasant to say so, we have shown that they have stolen it; come, let us present the Greeks themselves as witnesses of their own theft. For they, taking their own things from one another so openly, confirm that they are thieves, and yet, even unwillingly, they secretly show the truth from us to their fellow countrymen. For they will not even refrain from their own things, let alone ours. And I will be silent about the philosophical doctrines, since they themselves have written that they received the most important of their doctrines from Socrates, so that they may not seem ungrateful. Having used the testimonies of a few of the men who are esteemed among the Greeks, I will examine their plagiaristic type, using times indiscriminately, and I will proceed to the next things. Orpheus, then, having said: 'so there was not a more dog-like and more shaggy thing than a woman', Homer says openly: 'so there was not a more shameful and dog-like thing than a woman'. And having written: 'for art is always much better than strength', Homer says: 'is it not that the woodcutter is surrounded either by skill or by force?' Again, Musaeus having said: 'and just as the fertile earth produces leaves, some of which perish in the honeycombs, while others produce', Homer transcribes: 'leaves, some of which the wind scatters on the ground, while others the distant forest produces, and the season of spring comes; so also the generation and tribe of men are destroyed'. Again, Homer having said: 'it is not right for those who have acquired wealth to pray for men', Archilochus and Cratinus write, the former: 'for it is not good to insult men who have died', and Cratinus in The Lacians: 'this is a fearful thing for men, for those who have acquired wealth to boast greatly'. And again Archilochus, transferring that Homeric phrase: 'I am amazed, and I do not think it is unjust', writes in this way: 'I was blinded, and some other man was struck by this folly'; just as that phrase: 'common to all, and even the killer kills', he himself, having transformed it, brought it out in this way: 'I will act; for war is common to men'. Still, transferring another phrase: 'the victory of men is in the trial of the gods', through this iambic phrase it is clear: 'and he encouraged the young, and the limits of victory are in the gods'.

pass_b_english:
Before we begin the proposed task, we must supply what is lacking at the end of the fifth Stromata by way of an introduction. We have already shown that the symbolic mode is ancient, and that not only our prophets but also most of the ancient Greeks and many of the other barbarian nations have employed it. It was therefore also necessary to examine the mysteries of the initiations. I pass over these things for now, reserving their explanation for when we come to refute the doctrines about first principles that the Greeks have put forward. We will then show that both this theory and the mysteries belong to them. Having demonstrated the bent of the Greek mind, illuminated by the truth given to us through the Scriptures, and having indicated that they have received the stolen truth from us — if it is not offensive to say so — we have proved that they stole it. Come, then; let us bring forward the Greeks themselves as witnesses against themselves. For in openly taking their own ideas from one another, they confirm that they are thieves, yet even unwillingly they secretly pass on the truth that comes from us to their fellow countrymen. They will not even refrain from stealing from their own, let alone from us. I will keep silent about their philosophical doctrines, since the very men who handed down the schools admit in writing that they received the most important of their doctrines from Socrates, so that they might not appear ungrateful. Having cited the testimonies of a few men who were respected among the Greeks and who associated with them, I will expose their plagiaristic method, disregarding chronological order, and then proceed to what follows.

Orpheus, for instance, said: "So there was nothing more dog-like and more shaggy than a woman." Homer says outright: "So there was nothing more shameful and dog-like than a woman." And when Musaeus wrote: "For art is always far better than strength," Homer says: "Does not the woodcutter prevail either by skill or by force?" Again, Musaeus said: "And just as the fertile earth produces leaves, some of which perish in the honeycombs while others grow, so also the generation and tribe of men are destroyed." Homer transcribes it: "Leaves, some of which the wind scatters on the ground, while others the distant forest produces, and the season of spring comes; so also the generation of men, one grows while another perishes." Again, when Homer said: "It is not right for those who have acquired wealth to pray for men," Archilochus and Cratinus write — the former: "For it is not good to mock men who have died," and Cratinus in The Laconians: "This is a fearful thing for men, for those who have acquired wealth to boast greatly." And again Archilochus, transferring that Homeric phrase — "I am amazed, and I do not think it is unjust" — writes instead: "I was blinded, and some other man was struck by this folly." Just as with that line: "War is common to all, and the killer kills," he transforms it and brings it out as: "I will act; for war is common to men." Still, translating another phrase: "The victory of men lies in the trial of the gods," he makes it clear through this iambic line: "And he encouraged the young, and the limits of victory are in the gods."

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex Greek syntax, particularly the series of participial constructions and the poetic quotations. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek (e.g., 'if it is not unpleasant to say so' for 'εἰ μὴ ἐπαχθὲς εἰπεῖν'), and Pass B provides a fluent, equivalent rendering. All poetic comparisons (Orpheus/Homer, Musaeus/Homer, Homer/Archilochus/Cratinus) are correctly rendered in both versions. No omissions or misinterpretations of agency or modality were found.
